types.name: CapDraw
types.doc:
A polar-cap drawing instruction (mercator only).

A cap instruction covers a **longitude interval**, not a single column.
That makes the two regimes the same shape:

* one column wide (`spanLng == grid.tileWidthDeg`) — a crisp wedge
textured with that column's own tile;
* up to `360°` — a smeared strip textured with a single image, used when
the camera sits inside the cap.

members.name: request
members.doc:
Request a tile (idempotent; failures are graded, never blacklisted).

The tile is **enqueued** on the [TileScheduler] priority queue and a pump
dispatches as many as the concurrency gate allows. A tile that finds every
slot busy is no longer silently dropped (and re-requested next frame) — it
waits its turn and is dispatched the moment a slot frees.

members.name: resolve
members.doc:
Resolve one ideal tile: exact → descendants → ancestors.

The **ideal** tile is always requested (MapLibre `_updateRetainedTiles`
→ `_addTile(idealID)`), *even when a fallback is already drawable*. This
is not an optimisation detail: requesting only when nothing at all is
cached means that the moment a coarse tile is in the cache — which is
true after **every** zoom-in — the finer tile is never fetched and the
view stays pinned to the coarse level forever.

The **ancestor chain** is different: it escalates one level per round and
only after the level below has actually failed (MapLibre
`parentWasRequested`). Requesting the whole pyramid at once is what
produced request storms (and the black holes that followed).

members.name: drawsFor
members.doc:
The drawing commands for one ideal tile.

* exact hit → one command (whole texture);
* loaded descendants → one command per child (they tile the footprint);
* loaded ancestor → one command: the *fine* footprint with the
ancestor's sub-rectangle as texture region.

An empty list means "nothing available yet" — the caller keeps the
previous frame underneath so the screen never flashes black.

members.name: capDraws
members.doc:
The polar caps that should be drawn for the current camera.

Only mercator has a blind spot (|lat| > 85.05°); the cap stretches the
edge pixel row of the first / last tile row onto the pole.

Two regimes, chosen by [PolarCapBuilder.columnCountFor]:

* **wedge** — the span is a handful of columns wide: each column is drawn
as its own strip, textured with its own tile. Crisp, and the request
count is proportional to the visible cap.
* **smeared** — the span needs more columns than
[GeoEngineTuning.maxPolarCapColumns] allows (the camera is inside the
cap, so the arc wraps the pole): **one** strip, one image. Drawing a
wedge per column there meant 4096 meshes per frame, each with a
different picture, i.e. a sunburst across the whole viewport.

members.name: fadeOpacity
members.signature:
double fadeOpacity(TileImage image, int now) =>
selfFadeOpacity(image.loadedAt, now, fadeDurationMs)
members.doc:
Linear self-fade opacity (0→1) for [image] at wall-clock [now].

A `null` [TileImage.loadedAt] (e.g. a pre-cached image) is always 1. This
is the raster-only "load fade" of MapLibre — a tile is blended in from
transparent to opaque instead of popping in (see `draw_raster.ts`
`getSelfFadeValues`). The math lives in `geo_map_core` so it is
unit-testable without `dart:ui`.

types.name: TileLayer
types.doc:
Raster tile layer for both 2D and 3D.

### Engine ownership

The layer accepts an optional [engine]. When one is injected, **it belongs
to the host** and the layer must never dispose it: the whole point of the
shared engine is that the 2D and 3D layers trade places without dropping
the cache, and the layer that is being unmounted has no idea whether a
sibling is about to mount with the same engine.

Getting this backwards is not subtle — disposing the injected engine kills
every in-flight decode (`_decode` drops the frame on `_disposed`) and the
very next build asserts `A TileEngine was used after being disposed`, which
surfaces as "the globe basemap never loads".

members.name: TileLayer
engine
members.doc: The shared engine. When `null` the layer creates one and owns it.

members.doc:
Register (or replace) the features of one source.

[visible] hides the whole source without removing it — a layer that is
switched off must not be pickable. [pointRadiusPx] overrides the query's
default pick radius for this source, and [layerId] records which layer
it came from.

[popup] optionally binds a popup card to this source (the SDK equivalent of
MapLibre `map.on('click', layerId, handler)`); see [GeoPopupBinding]. A
source without a popup is still pickable — it just won't open a card via
[GeoPopupController] (the host may drive a SnackBar or selection instead).

types.name: GlobeImageLayer
types.doc:
Image overlay (weather radar, satellite swath, …) drawn on the globe.

flutter_map's `OverlayImageLayer` maps the image onto a quad from four
corners, which on a sphere looks like a flat sheet: no curvature, no horizon
clipping. This layer tessellates the bounds into a mesh and projects every
vertex, so the overlay follows the surface and disappears behind it.

types.name: GlobeProjectionDelegate
types.doc:
Orthographic globe projection plugged into flutter_map through the
(fork-only) `MapProjectionDelegate` hook.

Screen space replaces world space:
* `project()` returns **screen pixels** (or far-away coordinates for points
on the far side, so flutter_map's own culling removes them),
* `pixelOrigin` is forced to zero by the forked `MapCamera`,
* `pixelBounds` is the viewport.

members.name: maxCameraLatitude
members.doc:
The camera may look straight at a pole. 85.0511° is a **tile data** limit
(Web Mercator), not a projection limit — clamping the camera there makes
the globe feel truncated, so only stop just short of the degenerate pole.

members.name: radius
members.signature: double get radius => tileSize * math.pow(2, _zoom) / (2 * math.pi)
members.doc:
Disc radius in logical pixels — a function of zoom only.

Multiplying by `1/cos(lat)` (mercator's trick) would make the globe grow
as you drag towards the poles; on a sphere the apparent size is fixed.

types.doc:
Vector debug layer for the globe.

Deliberately **not** flutter_map's `PolylineLayer`/`PolygonLayer`: those
re-project with `crs.transform` after `camera.project`, which is wrong once
a projection delegate is in play. Here every vertex goes through
`camera.project` (the delegate) and great-circle densification, so the layer
also serves as the reference for what those layers will need later.

Densifies a path along great circles.

flutter_map's polygon/polyline painters connect projected points with
straight screen lines, so data fed to them must already be densified for the
edges to follow the sphere.

functions.name: buildGraticule
functions.doc:
Meridians every [lngStep]° and parallels every [latStep]°.

Parallels are sampled densely so they visibly curve — that curvature is the
first thing to check when the projection is off.

Tissot indicatrices: small equal-radius circles on the sphere.

On a correct orthographic projection they stay circular at the disc centre
and squash into ellipses towards the limb — an instant visual check for
distortion and for wrong great-circle interpolation.

types.name: HttpTileSource
types.doc:
WMTS / XYZ over HTTP.

URL building (templates, TMS flip, quadkey, bbox, subdomains, ratio) is
delegated to the pure [TileUrlBuilder] in core, so it is unit-tested there.
This class only owns the 404-vs-network failure split; the socket itself is
the shared transport in `platform/http_get.dart`, which has a browser
implementation so this file compiles for web.

[urlTemplate] supports `{z}`, `{x}`, `{y}`, `{TileMatrix}`, `{TileRow}`,
`{TileCol}`, `{prefix}`, `{ratio}`, `{quadkey}`, `{bbox}`,
`{bbox-epsg-3857}`. Both RESTful WMTS and plain XYZ templates work, e.g.:

```
WMTS (EPSG:4326, NASA GIBS):
https://gibs.earthdata.nasa.gov/wmts/epsg4326/best/MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_TrueColor/default/2026-10-20/250m/{z}/{y}/{x}.jpg

XYZ:
https://tile.openstreetmap.org/{z}/{x}/{y}.png
```

[dataZoom] is the level tiles are fetched at (0..source.maxZoom), which is

members.name: handleTap
members.signature:
List<GeoQueryHit> handleTap(
LatLng tap, {
required GeoMapController controller,
required GeoFeatureRegistry registry,
double? pointRadiusPx,
List<GeoQueryHit>? hits,
})
members.doc:
The single entry point for a map tap.

Queries [registry], filters to sources that registered a popup, and opens
the highest-priority one. No hit, or a hit on a source without a popup
(e.g. an airport that only fires a SnackBar), closes any open popup.

Pass [hits] when the host already ran the query (it usually needs the same
results for its own business reactions) — this avoids querying twice.

Disposed controller (see [isDisposed]) → no-op: the popup it owned no longer
exists, and the freshly created replacement will handle the next tap.

Returns the query result so the host can reuse it for its own reactions
(SnackBar / selection) without querying a second time.

members.name: pendingTimeoutMs

members.doc:
A missing tile (HTTP 404) stays missing for longer: MapLibre does not
blacklist it, it just falls back to parent/child tiles.

members.name: decodeFailureTtlMs
members.doc: Decode failures (corrupt payload) — retry, but not immediately.

members.name: failureBackoffBaseMs
members.doc:
Exponential backoff base for repeated failures of the same tile
(MapLibre `tile.ts`: `1000 * 2^(n-1)`).

members.name: failureBackoffMaxMs
members.doc: Cap for the exponential backoff.

members.name: maxPolarCapColumns
members.doc:
Upper bound on the number of **separate meshes** used to draw one polar
cap.

Two regimes exist and this constant is the switch between them:

* **wedge regime** (`columns ≤ maxPolarCapColumns`) — every visible grid
column gets its own strip textured with that column's own tile. This is
the crisp path and it is what a cap seen from *outside* looks like.
* **smeared regime** (`columns > maxPolarCapColumns`) — the whole visible
arc is drawn as **one** strip with a single texture. The camera is
inside the cap here, the arc wraps all the way around the pole, and a
per-column wedge would mean thousands of meshes each sampling a
different image: that is precisely the radial sunburst that used to
fill the viewport.

The bound therefore has to stay small enough that the wedge regime stays
cheap, and the smeared regime is only reached where the cap is a
featureless blob anyway.

members.name: featurePickRadiusPx
members.doc:
Default screen-space pick radius (px) for point features.

24 px is roughly twice the on-screen diameter of a 12 px symbol, so a
dot is grabbable without demanding pixel accuracy. Hosts may override it
per query or per feature.

members.name: hiddenPointSentinelPx
members.doc:
Magnitude at which a projected screen coordinate is treated as the
"not drawable" sentinel.

The globe projector returns `(-1e6, -1e6)` for the far side of the
sphere. Such a coordinate is finite, so a naive distance check would
treat it as "very far away" rather than "not pickable" — both are
rejected, but the sentinel must be detected explicitly.

members.name: featureBoundaryEpsilonDeg
members.doc:
Tolerance (degrees) for "the tap is exactly on the ring boundary".

1e-7° is about a centimetre — it only absorbs floating-point noise, it
does not widen the shape.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: TileFailureKind
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Why a tile could not be produced.

The distinction matters: a missing tile (404) must **not** be blacklisted
(MapLibre `tile_manager.ts` `_loadTile` just calls `update()` again and
keeps falling back to parent/child tiles), while a network error is
transient and should be retried quickly.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: TileFetchResult
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
The outcome of a single tile fetch.

MapLibre draws a hard line between "the server says there is no such tile"
(404 — never blacklisted, the engine keeps falling back) and "the request
broke" (network error — retried quickly). Collapsing both into `null` is
what made the old engine blacklist tiles after two failures.

members.name: bytes
members.doc: The decoded payload, or `null` when [failure] is set.

members.name: failure
members.doc: Why the tile could not be produced (`null` on success).

members.name: isOk
members.signature: bool get isOk => failure == null && bytes != null

geo_map_core_reexport.name: TileRowOrder
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Row order used **on the wire**.

The internal (canonical) row order is always XYZ — row 0 is the northern
edge of the grid. Some services (TMS, MBTiles) number rows from the south,
so the row index must be flipped when a URL is built or a row is read from
a local file.

MapLibre does the same in one line: `tile_id.ts` L48
`y = scheme === 'tms' ? 2^z - y - 1 : y`.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: normalizeRingWinding
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Reverse the rings whose winding matches the outer ring's.

Canvas fills with the nonzero rule, so a hole wound like its outer ring
does **not** punch through; reversing it restores the hole. The outer ring
keeps its orientation, and a single-ring polygon is returned unchanged.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: parseGeoJsonFeatures
geo_map_core_reexport.doc: Parse a GeoJSON `FeatureCollection` or a single `Feature`.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: pointInMultiPolygon
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Whether [point] lies inside any sub-polygon of [polygons] (MultiPolygon).

The sub-polygons are evaluated independently (union semantics), which
matches how the renderer draws them — one `addPolygon` per ring.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: pointInPolygon
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Whether [point] lies inside the polygon [rings] (first ring = outer ring,
the rest = holes).

The interior is "outer ring minus holes" (RFC 7946). Boundary handling:
a point on the **outer** boundary counts as inside; a point on a **hole's**
boundary counts as outside — the hole wins.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: pointInRing
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Whether [point] lies inside the closed ring [ring].

Uses the even-odd rule, so the ring's winding does not matter.
[includeBoundary] decides whether a point exactly on an edge counts as
inside (default: yes).

Returns `false` for rings with fewer than three vertices.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: ringSignedArea
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Signed area of [ring], measured on **unwrapped** longitudes.

Positive means counter-clockwise. Unwrapping matters: a ring near ±180°
would otherwise flip sign and silently change which ring is treated as the
outer one.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: splitRingAtSeam
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Split [ring] on the meridian [seamLng], returning one or two closed pieces.

The ring is unwrapped first, so a +179°/−179° edge is recognised as crossing
the seam. If the ring lies entirely on one side, `[ring]` is returned
unchanged. Pieces with fewer than three vertices are dropped.

This mirrors how MapLibre splits GeoJSON at ±180° during tiling. The
renderer itself only needs [unwrapLongitudes] plus world copies; this helper
keeps that behaviour testable and lets callers clip explicitly.

geo_map_core_reexport.name: unwrapLongitudes
geo_map_core_reexport.doc:
Sequentially unwrap [lons] so every consecutive delta stays in (-180, 180].

`out[0] == lons[0]`; `out[i] = out[i-1] + wrapLongitude(lons[i] - lons[i-1])`.
A ring that "jumps" from +179° to −179° becomes +179° → +181° (a 2° step)
instead of a −358° step, so it can be projected continuously.
